extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / wartime public and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A contemporary newspaper report of the Guadalcanal/Tulagi naval battles and associated political/military reactions, including statements by President Roosevelt and Secretary Knox about operational security and strategic implications. Focuses on battlefield outcomes, personnel losses, strategic significance, and wartime information policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold reporting of naval losses for operational security
rubrics_metrics.description: President Roosevelt defended the administration's policy of withholding news of naval losses "until it is clear that the enemy already has possession of the information" and confessed yielding to public clamor when a carrier sinking was disclosed prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress or delay public release of details about losses if disclosure would give the enemy actionable intelligence; release full details only when it is clear the enemy cannot exploit them. Example in text: an American carrier was torpedoed and later sank but news was withheld until the risk of aiding the enemy passed. Tradeoff: operational security vs. public demand for information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loose talk about operations ('Loose Talk Costs Lives')
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reiterates wartime admonitions such as the posters that say 'Loose Talk Costs Lives' and Roosevelt's warning that loose talk delays victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public and service members should refrain from sharing operational details or rumors; informal disclosures can endanger lives and delay victory. The phrase functions as a behavioral standard to reduce inadvertent leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of wartime unity: 'time only for working and fighting'
rubrics_metrics.description: Roosevelt asserted there was 'time only for working and fighting, none for exultation' and urged keeping politics out of the war while shelving long-range social reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During major campaigns, political disputes and nonessential reforms should be deprioritized to focus national effort on military objectives. This is a policy/normative criterion for leaders and institutions during wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning-point assessment criteria for major engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Roosevelt characterized successes in Africa and the Far Pacific as an apparent 'turning point of this war,' grounding that judgment in major enemy losses and strategic gains such as possession of Guadalcanal and its airfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a battle is a 'turning point' by considering: territory gained (e.g., control of Henderson Field/Guadalcanal), scale of enemy losses (ships sunk/damaged, troop casualties), effect on enemy operational capability, and cumulative effects across theaters. Caution: claims may be revised as fuller reports arrive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battle outcome metrics: counts of ships sunk/damaged and personnel losses
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece repeatedly uses enumerations (e.g., '23 ships sunk and 7 damaged', later tallies such as 'twenty-three Nipponese ships were sunk, seven were damaged') and estimated troop losses (e.g., 'possibly 20,000 to 40,000 Japanese troops') as primary measures of victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ship and troop loss tallies to quantify battle results, but note potential duplication or revision of figures; totals announced by different headquarters or broadcasts may conflict and require consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess naval superiority by industrial capacity and operational geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary Knox emphasized that American capacity 'for building many ships fast' helps offset losses, while the Japanese advantage lies in operating close to home waters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate long-term naval strength by weighing shipbuilding/industrial throughput against the enemy's logistical/geographical advantages. Short-term losses may be mitigated by superior production capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical assessment: effectiveness of surface forces alongside air units
rubrics_metrics.description: The article recounts naval tactics (American force splitting into columns, surface ships and cruisers engaging at close range) and notes commentators' view that 'the mightiest of naval surface weapons still had a place in modern warfare despite ... offensive power of aircraft.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing tactics, consider combined effects of surface gunfire, torpedoes, destroyer actions, and air strikes; evaluate maneuvers (e.g., splitting into columns, night engagements) for daring and effectiveness in achieving decisive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition criteria for decorations and citations for ships/crews
rubrics_metrics.description: The text mentions recommendations that a ship (the San Francisco) 'be the first of our Navy's vessels to be decorated' for outstanding service, while noting there were 'no medals... which carry such high honor' at the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award citations/decorations based on extraordinary performance in battle (e.g., leading assault into enemy fire, saving ship, significant contribution to victory). Administrative delays or policy constraints may affect timing and form of recognition.
